title: Matrimony
hook: in the Latin Church the couple are the ministers; they give the sacrament to each other

segments.voice: Yesterday, ordination: deacons, priests and bishops, and hands laid on in silence. Your line was called to serve.

Here's a trivia question that surprises most Catholics: at a Catholic wedding, who gives the sacrament? Most people would say the priest. He's the one in vestments, standing in the middle, asking the questions. But in the Latin Church, the answer is the bride and the groom. The priest or deacon is there as the Church's witness. The two people holding hands are the ones doing it. They give the sacrament to each other. Today, the last of the seven: matrimony.
screen: `WHO GIVES THE SACRAMENT?` → `NOT THE PRIEST.` → `THE BRIDE AND THE GROOM.`

segments.voice: Matrimony comes from Latin, matrimonium, built on mater, mother: an old Roman word, looking ahead to family. In the Latin Church, the heart of the sacrament is consent: two people freely saying yes to each other, for life, in front of witnesses. That's why the couple are the ministers. Their promise is the sign. The priest or deacon asks, blesses, and receives the vows for the Church. The Eastern churches understand it differently: the priest's blessing is essential, and the couple are crowned, as a king and queen of a new little kingdom. Jesus speaks about marriage in Matthew's Gospel, going back to Genesis. In the Douay-Rheims: "Therefore now they are not two, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let no man put asunder." Paul, writing to the Ephesians about husbands and wives, says in the same translation, "This is a great sacrament; but I speak in Christ and in the church." The Latin Bible used the word sacramentum there, and it helped shape how the Church came to see marriage: a human love that shows God's own faithful love. Catholics understand it as lifelong, faithful, and open to children. So the Church doesn't recognize divorce as ending a valid marriage, though it can declare, after careful review, that a marriage was never valid to begin with. Other Christians see marriage in different ways: many Protestant churches treat it as holy but not a sacrament, and the Orthodox, in some cases, allow a second marriage. That completes the seven: three to bring you in, two to heal, two to serve.
screen: `MATRIMONIUM, FROM MATER, MOTHER.` · `THE COUPLE ARE THE MINISTERS.` · `NOT TWO, BUT ONE FLESH.` · `THIS IS A GREAT SACRAMENT.` · then, large: `TWO MINISTERS, ONE PROMISE.`

segments.voice: Think of two people you know who have been together a long time, grandparents, parents, neighbors or friends, and picture them on an ordinary day: one making coffee, the other reading out the news. Think of what it's taken to keep that promise through the bad years, the sick years, the funny ones. If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, just be glad for them.
Matrimony. From the Latin for mother. The sacrament two people give each other, with their own promise. Today's word.
Your line: two ministers, one promise. That's all seven sacraments: baptism, confirmation, Eucharist, reconciliation, anointing, orders, matrimony. Day one hundred thirty-two, done.

howItsDone: Catholics usually marry at a Mass or wedding service in church, exchanging vows before a priest or deacon and two witnesses, after a period of marriage preparation with the parish.
